notes:
Need to search first.I've written verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 29 below, but some of what you asked for is missing. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through. I found nothing from Lutheran, Orthodox, NET Bible or Bible Odyssey sources, and nothing from Spurgeon, Ligonier or The Gospel Coalition, so those are left out. Most notes come from the older commentaries, the Enduring Word commentary by David Guzik, and Haydock's Catholic commentary. In some cases I saw only the short excerpt the search returned, not the whole page.

**Main sources (short names used below)**
- EW = Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-29/
- MH = Matthew Henry: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_029.cfm
- Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-29.html
- Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-29.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/29.htm
- Gill (StudyLight labels him Baptist and Calvinist): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-29.html
- Wesley (StudyLight labels him Wesleyan/Methodist and Arminian): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-29.html
- Haydock (Catholic, 1811): https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-29.html
- Expositor's Bible: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/isaiah/29.htm
- BH Study = Bible Hub's chapter study page: https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/29.htm

---

**v. 1**
- **What "Ariel" means:** Guzik thinks the best reading is "Lion of God," used sarcastically. Jerusalem may have given itself this proud name, but God didn't agree with it. He also says the city leaned on its past ("where David camped") and lived for present pleasures. (EW)
- **Other explanations of the name:**
  - Ellicott calls it a poetic nickname, like "Rahab," that Isaiah may have made up himself. (Ellicott)
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls it a coded name for Jerusalem. It says most explain it as "lion of God," but notes that Delitzsch suggested "hearth of God" or "altar of God," as in Ezekiel 43:15. (Pulpit, biblehub)
  - Bible Hub's study page says the word plays on both senses, majestic and easily burned. (BH Study)
- **The festivals:** Ellicott says "year to year" points to keeping the New Year festival, which could not stop the coming trouble. (Ellicott) Wesley says the sacrifices were offered to calm God's anger, "but all shall be in vain." (Wesley)
- **Gill:** Gill notes that Jewish writers and the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) take Ariel as the altar of burnt offering. He suggests the line may mean "the feasts shall be cut off." (Gill)
- **Which siege is meant? (a real difference):**
  - Matthew Henry sees mainly the Assyrian siege, but says it also applies to the later Babylonian and Roman destructions. (MH)
  - Gill reads verses 1–8 mainly as the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. (Gill)
  - Haydock mentions the Babylonians and the Romans, but also says Sennacherib's invasion is foretold here. (Haydock)
- **Modern reading:** The Expositor's Bible discusses a reading of the line as "city which David beleaguered," that is, a city David himself once besieged, offered as a precedent for God besieging his own city. (Expositor's)

**v. 2**
- **What "like an altar hearth" means (a split):**
  - Calvin and Gill say the whole city will be like the altar, running with the blood of the slain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/29-2.html; Gill)
  - Clarke and Barnes say the reverse: Jerusalem becomes the altar fire where God's *enemies* are burned up. (same StudyLight 29-2 page)
  - Haydock agrees with that second view: Sennacherib's army was offered up like a sacrifice. (Haydock)
- Matthew Henry's alternative: if the people repent, Jerusalem will be "a holy city" again. (StudyLight 29-2)
- **Pulpit:** Cheyne's translation "moaning and bemoaning" captures the Hebrew wordplay. The siege was a punishment "far more in love than in wrath," meant to bring repentance. (Pulpit)
- **Ellicott:** Translate it "But she shall be unto me as Ariel." The city will live up to its name even in sorrow. (Ellicott)
- **Ancient Greek translation (Septuagint):** It reads differently here: "her strength and her wealth shall be mine." (https://ccel.org/b/brenton/lxx/htm/12.xxix.htm)

**v. 3**
- Ellicott says this describes an Eastern siege as shown in Assyrian sculptures: an earth mound against the walls and a battering ram on top. (Ellicott)
- Matthew Henry says the enemy pitched the camp, but God says *he* does it, because they are his instrument. (MH) Gill makes the same point and links it to Luke 19:43. (Gill)
- Haydock notes Sennacherib never actually besieged the city (Isaiah 37:33), though he prepared to. (Haydock)
- The Septuagint reads "I will compass thee about like David." (ccel Brenton)

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the proud city's loud boasts are brought down to a whisper. (EW)
- **The "spirit from the ground":**
  - Ellicott: the people will whisper like the ghost-voices at fortune-tellers' séances (see Isaiah 8:19), probably during Sennacherib's invasion. (Ellicott)
  - Wesley: like oracles spoken from caves; the once-proud city will beg its enemies for favour. (Wesley)
  - Gill: a fitting punishment for people who consulted spirit-mediums. (Gill)
  - Haydock: "the Python," meaning a diviner. (Haydock)

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the city was lying in the dust; now its *enemies* become fine dust. (EW)
- Ellicott: the trouble will be short, and a sudden disaster, probably the destruction of Sennacherib's army, will bring the enemy low. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: God mixes promise in with warning. (Pulpit)
- Wesley differs: the "strangers" are foreigners Jerusalem *hired* to help it, as it did when the Babylonians came. (Wesley)
- Bible Hub's study page links this to the angel striking down 185,000 Assyrians (Isaiah 37:36). (BH Study)

**v. 6 — who is "visited"? (a clear split)**
- **On the enemies:** The Pulpit says the context shows the visitation falls on Judah's enemies, and the language is probably figurative. (Pulpit) Ellicott says it could be a literal storm acting as an "angel of the Lord," saving Jerusalem and destroying the besiegers. (Ellicott)
- **On Jerusalem:** Wesley reads "Thou, O Jerusalem." (Wesley) Gill says Jerusalem itself is punished, with the Romans as God's instruments. (Gill)
- Matthew Henry thinks "great noise" may mean they would be more frightened than hurt. (MH)

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik: the attackers dream of satisfaction and wake up unsatisfied. (EW)
- Ellicott: the enemies thought the prey was already theirs, but woke still empty. "The lion of Judah" would not be eaten by "the strong bull of Assyria." (Ellicott)
- Gill: "all the nations" means the Roman army drawn from many nations. (Gill)
- Wesley reads v. 8 differently: the enemies stay unsatisfied, always "thirsting after more of your blood." (Wesley)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary applies it to the world's hostility to the church: such plans will always fail. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-29.html)

**v. 9**
- **Ellicott:** better translated "Astonish yourselves." Picture the prophet reciting the prophecy to people who don't believe it. The verb form shows their stunned unbelief was their own doing. (Ellicott)
- **Pulpit:** "stand stupefied." The prophet tells them to act as he knows they will. (Pulpit)
- **Matthew Henry:** they were drunk with love of pleasure and with prejudice against religion. (MH)
- **Wesley:** they stagger like drunks who can't see their danger. (Wesley)
- **Popular modern teaching:** Guzik says this drunkenness was a *curse*, partly brought on themselves and partly sent by God. He applies this against people who teach that God "blesses" believers by making them "drunk in the Spirit." (EW)

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** God poured out deep sleep, which leaves people unproductive, vulnerable and insensitive. In silencing the prophets, God gave the people what they wanted. (EW)
- **Ellicott:** calling the seers "heads" is ironic, because they could not see. (Ellicott)
- **Pulpit:** the sleep here is "spiritual deadness," not rest. (Pulpit)
- **Wesley:** hardness of heart. (Wesley)
- **Matthew Henry:** links it to Romans 11:8 and sees it fulfilled when the chief priests and scribes opposed Christ. (MH)
- **Haydock (Catholic):** also cites Romans 11:8 and Chrysostom ("obstinacy"). The Jews only dimly understood what the prophets said about a coming Redeemer. (Haydock)

**vv. 11–12**
- **Guzik:** spiritual illiteracy. Even the man who could read found God's vision a sealed book. (EW)
- **Ellicott:**
  - "The whole vision" means all of Isaiah's teaching, compared with Revelation 5:2.
  - The educated treated it as closed.
  - The uneducated had a more genuine, less guilty excuse.
  (Ellicott)
- **Gill:** the prophecies about the Messiah. Neither learned nor unlearned searched the Scriptures. (Gill)
- **Benson (Wesleyan):** human learning without supernatural light cannot rightly understand God's word. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/29-11.htm)
- **Church Pulpit Commentary:** the Bible is "sealed" until its Author opens it, and the Spirit's help, promised to all who pray, puts rich and poor on the same level. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/isaiah-29.html)
- **Pulpit Homiletics:** God's word becomes sealed through human stubbornness and prejudice. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/isaiah/29.htm)
- **Latter-day Saint view:** GotQuestions reports that Mormon theologians point to this passage as a precedent for the "sealed portion" of the Book of Mormon plates. (https://www.gotquestions.org/The-Sealed-Portion.html)

**v. 13**
- **Guzik:** they talked spiritual talk while their hearts were far away. The people moved away, not God, and their fear of God was only commanded by men. Jesus rebuked the same pattern. (EW)
- **Ellicott:** an early form of Pharisee religion: a growing traditional system ending in dishonest hair-splitting and formal devotion. (Ellicott)
- **Pulpit:** the problem was not too much outward religion but no inward religion to match it. (Pulpit)
- **Wesley:** worship based on human inventions and false prophets' traditions. (Wesley)
- **Matthew Henry:** they valued the "tradition of the elders" above God's law. (MH)
- **Biblical Illustrator:** a human rule "learned by rote." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/29-13.html)
- **Preacher's Homiletical:** human authority in religion is "distinctly denounced." (same page)
- **Expositor's Bible:** they repeated other men's thoughts about God instead of knowing him. (Expositor's)
- **Jesus' use:** Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 15:8–9 and Mark 7:6–7. (https://biblehub.com/isaiah/29-13.htm)
- **Catholic reading:** Haydock notes the Gospel writers follow the Septuagint wording, and applies the verse to the Jews, who he says "still continue to corrupt God's word" by false interpretation. (Haydock)
- **Protestant–Catholic tension:** Precept Austin's Mark 7 page lists a GotQuestions article on whether Catholic tradition outranks the Bible as a related link. I did not read that article. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary)

**v. 14**
- **Guzik:** God destroys the wise men's wisdom that encouraged the pride. He ties this to Paul in 1 Corinthians 1. (EW; https://enduringword.com/right-kind-of-wisdom/) Bible Hub notes Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 1:19. (BH Study)
- **Matthew Henry:** they removed their hearts from God, so God removed wisdom from them. He sees this fulfilled after Israel rejected the gospel. (MH)
- **Haydock:** first, the politicians were confused when Sennacherib approached. Later, the Jews' blindness to prophecies fulfilled in Christ is itself the marvel. (Haydock)
- **Expositor's Bible:** the "marvellous work" is a political outcome showing God's wisdom, not a natural disaster. (Expositor's)

**v. 15**
- **Ellicott:**
  - This adds to the list of woes in Isaiah 5.
  - It probably refers to secret deals with Egypt or other powers instead of trusting God.
  (Ellicott)
- **Matthew Henry:** at bottom, a practical disbelief that God sees everything. (MH)
- **Wesley:** "dig deep" is a picture of burying something. (Wesley)
- **Homiletics:** hiding from God meant hiding from his prophet's rebuke. (biblehub homiletics)

**v. 16**
- **Ellicott:** read it as "O your perversity!" and "Shall the potter be counted as the clay?" They reversed Creator and creature and acted as practical atheists. (Ellicott)
- **Wesley (older King James wording):** their schemes are no more to God than clay is to the potter. (Wesley)
- **Matthew Henry:** hiding from God amounts to denying he made us. (MH)
- **Guzik:** applies it to modern claims that chance, not an intelligent Creator, made the universe. (EW)
- **Pulpit (citing Cheyne):** cross-references Romans 9:20. (Pulpit)
- **On the potter image:** Ellicott says it suggests a love that will fulfil itself, not an arbitrary sovereignty. (Ellicott, v. 17)

**v. 17 — what the reversal refers to (a split)**
- **The calling of the Gentiles:** Wesley says it foretells "the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles." (Wesley) Gill says the uncultivated Gentile world becomes a fruitful field through the gospel. (Gill) Clarke takes a similar view. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/29-17.html)
- **Nearer events first:** Matthew Henry sees first the peace after Sennacherib's defeat, then possibly the Gentiles' entry into the church. (MH)
- **The Messiah's kingdom:** Coffman says it points to the Messiah's kingdom, for the faithful remnant. (StudyLight 29-17)
- **Restoration:** Ellicott sees a restoration of both nature and human life. (Ellicott)
- **A picture of politics:** the Expositor's Bible calls it a metaphor for God overturning human politics. (Expositor's)

**v. 18**
- **Ellicott:** the open vision here contrasts with the self-chosen ignorance of v. 11. The "scroll" may be Isaiah's message or the Law. (Ellicott)
- **Matthew Henry:** "The fulfilling of prophecy is the best exposition of it." (MH)
- **Wesley:** brought by grace into saving knowledge. (Wesley)
- **Bible Hub:** links it to Jesus' ministry in Matthew 11:5. (BH Study)

**v. 19**
- Wesley: the "poor" are people the Jews looked down on, such as the Gentiles and most of the first Christians. (Wesley)
- Haydock: Jesus alludes to this verse in Luke 7:22, pointing to the calling of the Gentiles. (Haydock)
- Bible Hub: echoed in Mary's song. (BH Study)

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: the mockers at home are removed by Hezekiah's reform. (MH)
- Haydock: Hezekiah promoted piety more zealously after the deliverance. (Haydock)
- Wesley: "look for evil" means people who are eager to practise wickedness. (Wesley)

**v. 21**
- **Ellicott:** Isaiah himself was probably accused of being unpatriotic, and the false charges were "chaotic" (*tohu*, the same word as "without form" in Genesis 1). (Ellicott)
- **Pulpit:** sets out other translations (Kay, Cheyne, Delitzsch) and keeps the traditional sense of punishing someone for mere words. The "gate" was the court, where anyone who rebuked the oppressors was trapped. (Pulpit, biblehub)
- **Matthew Henry, quoted in Homiletics:** they twisted every word the prophets said. He applies it to the chief priests who persecuted Christ. (biblehub homiletics; MH)
- **Haydock:** "the just" means Christ. (Haydock)

**v. 22**
- Matthew Henry and Wesley: God redeemed Abraham from the idolatry of Ur. (MH; Wesley)
- Wesley: Jacob's descendants will finally return to their Messiah. (Wesley)
- Ellicott: pictures Jacob watching over his descendants, now seeing a brighter day. (Ellicott)

**v. 23**
- Wesley: the "children" are Gentiles born to God through the gospel and joined with Israel in one body. (Wesley)
- Matthew Henry: children are God's workmanship, which comforts parents. (MH)

**v. 24**
- **Pulpit (citing Delitzsch):** refers to recent grumbling resistance to God's warnings, not Israel's complaining in the wilderness. The grumblers will gladly receive the prophets' teaching. (Pulpit, biblehub)
- **Wesley:** Gentiles who strayed. (Wesley)
- **Gill:** they come to understand Christ, and the grumbling had been against Christ. (Gill)
- **Septuagint:** adds a line saying "stammering tongues shall learn to speak peace." (ccel Brenton)
